replacements.old_body: On September 23, 1889, according to Nintendo's corporate documentation, Fusajiro Yamauchi founded the Kyoto business that would become Nintendo, devoted to the production and sale of hanafuda cards. The date is important because it distinguishes the historical founding from the incorporation of the modern company in 1947. Over the following decades, Nintendo moved through Western-style playing cards, toys, arcade systems and electronics before becoming one of the world's major video game companies. This long transformation is not an inevitable line toward consoles, but a succession of experiments, skills and market changes. From hanafuda to Game & Watch, from Famicom to Wii, however, one question keeps returning: how can an object and a rule become a gesture people want to repeat?
replacements.heading: The Kyoto playing-card business
replacements.body: Nintendo was founded as Yamauchi Nintendo (山内任天堂) by Fusajiro Yamauchi on September 23, 1889, though it was originally named Nintendo Koppai. Based in Kyoto, Japan, the business produced and marketed hanafuda, a type of Japanese playing card. The name "Nintendo" is commonly assumed to mean "leave luck to heaven", but there are no historical records to validate this. Hanafuda cards were an alternative to Western-style playing cards which were banned in Japan at the time. Nintendo's cards gained popularity, so Yamauchi hired assistants to mass-produce them.

replacements.old_body: Hanafuda cards use pictorial motifs and combinations that require familiarity with a shared system. Producing them means making an object that comes alive through rules and through people gathered around a table. This origin matters without needing to turn it into a prophecy of consoles. The technology is different, and so is the commercial context. Yet it remains a concrete example of how an entertainment product is not identical to the material from which it is made. Cards have to be used, interpreted and placed in relation to one another. Their quality supports a social practice. Nintendo's history therefore begins with a physical object whose value also depends on what people know how to do together through it.
replacements.heading: Hanafuda: pictures on playing cards
replacements.body: Hanafuda (花札; lit. 'flower cards') are a type of Japanese playing cards. They are typically smaller than Western playing cards, only 5.4 by 3.2 centimetres (2.1 by 1.3 in), but thicker and stiffer. On the face of each card is a depiction of plants, tanzaku (短冊; 'paper strips'), animals, birds, or man-made objects. One single card depicts a human. The back side is usually plain, without a pattern or design of any kind, and traditionally colored either red or black. Hanafuda are used to play a variety of games including Koi-Koi and Hachi-Hachi.

replacements.old_heading: 1966 / Toys that move in your hands
replacements.old_body: The expansion into toys opens a different relationship with gesture. Objects such as the Ultra Hand tie fun to a mechanical transformation that is easy to understand: the player acts and immediately sees a consequence. This immediacy helps explain an important thread in the company's history, in which a technical possibility is made accessible through a concrete form. Not every experiment leads to lasting success, and the path is not linear. The work also consists of recognizing which interactions can sustain interest beyond the first surprise. The toy therefore becomes a laboratory for the relationship between hand and object. Before a long explanation, there has to be something a person can try and understand directly with their own body.
replacements.heading: Gunpei Yokoi and the extending Ultra Hand
replacements.body:
Ultra Hand is a toy that was manufactured by Nintendo in the late 1960s. It was created in 1966 by Gunpei Yokoi, who later designed the Love Tester, the D-pad, the Game & Watch, the Game Boy, and the WonderSwan.

Ultra Hand consists of several criss-cross-connected plastic elements, and operates on the "lazy tongs" pantograph principle. One end of the Ultra Hand has scissor-like handles and is operated like scissors, extending when the handles are pinched together and retracting when they are parted.  On the other end of the Ultra Hand are two bowl-shaped grips with which ball-like objects can be gripped when the Ultra Hand is fully extended. Three colored balls were included in the Ultra Hand package, along with stands on which the balls can rest.

replacements.old_body: With electronic entertainment, part of the rules is executed by the device instead of being managed entirely by the participants. This transition changes the company's craft: systems now have to respond, represent a state and make change readable. Early machines and electronic games belong to a phase of experimentation in which Nintendo is looking for a place within a new sector. The result depends not only on the available components, but on how they are organized to create an understandable experience. Here the history gains a material continuity with later video games. The hand still acts on an object, but the object can now retain conditions and produce behavior more complex than a simple mechanical response.

replacements.old_body: In 1980, Nintendo developed and released Game & Watch, bringing video games into a pocket-sized object with an LCD screen, essential controls and a clock function that justified the device's everyday presence. Portability does not only reduce the size of the screen: it changes the amount of time available for play. Actions have to be understood quickly, sessions can be interrupted and resumed, and the score becomes a compact memory of performance. This logic prepares ground that Nintendo would continue to explore with Game Boy and later handheld consoles. The point is not to reproduce an arcade in miniature, but to design around the real conditions of the object: battery, display, few buttons and short moments taken from the day.
replacements.heading: Game & Watch: a game and a clock
replacements.body: In addition to the arcade games, Nintendo was testing the consumer handheld video game market with the Game & Watch. It is a line of handheld electronic games produced by Nintendo from 1980 to 1991. Created by Gunpei Yokoi, each Game & Watch features a single game to be played on an LCD screen in addition to a clock or an alarm. It is the earliest Nintendo product to garner major success, with 43.4 million units sold worldwide.

replacements.old_body: In 1983, Nintendo launched the Family Computer, or Famicom, in Japan. The shift is decisive because the company is no longer producing only individual electronic devices: it is building a home platform on which software can accumulate, differentiate itself and create lasting habits. The value of the machine therefore also depends on its catalogue and on the relationship between hardware, controller and games. In the following years, titles such as Super Mario Bros. would show how a console can establish a shared grammar without making experiences identical. Standardized controls become a base on which creators design variations. Nintendo thus enters a different industrial form, in which designing a machine also means organizing a production and commercial environment capable of sustaining many games over time.
replacements.heading: Famicom and the Nintendo Entertainment System
replacements.body:
In 1983, Nintendo released their first cartridge-based game console, the Family Computer or "Famicom", in Japan. More than 500,000 units were sold within two months. After a few months of favorable sales, Nintendo received complaints that some Famicom consoles would freeze on certain games. The fault was found in a malfunctioning chip and Nintendo decided to recall all Famicom units that were currently on store shelves.

It was renamed the "Nintendo Entertainment System" (NES), the phrase "entertainment system" intentionally used to avoid sounding like a console. Its games were referred to by Nintendo as "game paks" [sic] instead of cartridges, and they were inserted into a "control deck" instead of a console. To look similar to contemporary entertainment devices such as VCRs and stereo systems, the NES had a gray, boxy design with a "futuristic aesthetic". The company created R.O.B., a robot-shaped peripheral for the console, to market it as having another aspect than the games themselves.

replacements.old_heading: Between a frame and a choice
replacements.old_body: Cinema chooses where we look; a game must also account for what we decide to do. In Hideo Kojima's work, these languages meet frequently, without always seeking a comfortable resolution. Explore the relationship between staging and interaction: a pause, a voice or a gesture can change how we inhabit a sequence, rather than simply watch it.
replacements.heading: Hideo Kojima: designer, writer and director
replacements.body: Hideo Kojima (小島 秀夫, Kojima Hideo; born August 24, 1963) is a Japanese video game designer, writer, director, and producer. He is best known for the Metal Gear franchise, which remains his most famous and acclaimed work. His games are noted for being highly cinematic, the result of a passion for film and literature which began during his childhood, and he is regarded as a pioneering auteur of video games.

replacements.old_body: Capcom's origins predate its modern image as a global publisher. The company emerged within Japanese electronic entertainment and grew as arcades became a rapid laboratory for rules, difficulty and visual attraction. In that market, every game had to communicate immediately and persuade the audience to try again. This pressure contributed to a design culture attentive to control response and readability. Many skills Capcom later brought to consoles were refined in an environment where player feedback was direct, public and measurable. This passage explains why Capcom remains interesting beyond its date. corporate origins and arcades is not isolated, but a node connecting production, rules and player perception inside the same experience.
replacements.heading: From electronic game machines to Capcom
replacements.body: The original companies that spawned Capcom's Japan branch were I.R.M. and its subsidiary Japan Capsule Computers Co., Ltd., both of which were devoted to the manufacture and distribution of electronic game machines. The two companies underwent a name change to Sanbi Co., Ltd. in September 1981. On June 11, 1983, Tsujimoto established Capcom Co., Ltd. to take over the internal sales department.

replacements.old_heading: Lua Is Born Small Enough to Live Inside Other Programs
replacements.old_body: On July 28, 1993 Lua 1.0 was already running at PUC-Rio. This was not a commercial release: the official version history notes that the first version was never publicly released, but the date marks the language's concrete existence. Designed to be embedded inside other systems, Lua favors small size, portability and flexible data structures. Those qualities would later make it valuable in games, where rules, interfaces and content often need to change without rebuilding an entire engine.
replacements.heading: Lua: a language embedded in applications
replacements.body:
Lua  is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications. Lua is cross-platform software, since the interpreter of compiled bytecode is written in ANSI C, and Lua has a relatively simple C application programming interface (API) to embed it into applications.

Lua originated in 1993 as a language for extending software applications to meet the increasing demand for customization at the time. It provided the basic facilities of most procedural programming languages, but more complicated or domain-specific features were not included; rather, it included mechanisms for extending the language, allowing programmers to implement such features. As Lua was intended to be a general embeddable extension language, the designers of Lua focused on improving its speed, portability, extensibility and ease-of-use in development.
